note: Decision 0059: Earth's water table and the aquifer rating Hydrate or Diedrate reads. Every ground material of ground-rules-v1.json has a permeability class (the amendment agreed in the habitat proposal, 3a); a test checks that none is missing. k: the water table's depth per metre of height above the drainage base (the habitat prototype's v1 rule: clay .3, loam .55, sand .9). conductivity: the hydraulic conductivity of the class near the ground, m/day (geometric middles of the ranges in Heath 1983, USGS Water-Supply Paper 2220, and Freeze and Cherry 1979, table 2.2); a chunk's transmissivity is conductivity x saturated metres (see rating).

classes._note: conductivity m/day. Very low: clay, shale, unfractured crystalline rock (1e-7 to 1e-3). Low: till, silt, loess (1e-6 to 1). Peat: decomposed peat below the living layer (0.01 to 0.1). Fractured: the jointed top of crystalline rock (1e-4 to 10; hard-rock wells there give 1 to 50 m2/day). Medium: sandstone, conglomerate, basalt, regolith (1e-2 to 10 fractured or weakly cemented). Karst: fissured and cavernous limestone and dolomite (0.1 to 1000). High: sand (1 to 100) and gravel (10 to 1000).

materials._note: Ground-column materials (ground-rules-v1.json). Very low: raw clays, marl, mud, claystone, shale, slate, phyllite, oozes, frozen ground, unfractured crystalline rock. Low: tills, silt, loess, colluvium, weathered rock and crusts. Medium: topsoil, sandstone, conglomerate, basalt, regolith. High: sand and gravel. Karst: soluble rock.

rocks._note: rock-NAME blocks (vanilla, regional geology, other mods) whose name is not a ground material. Marbles are metamorphic carbonates: little karst. Unknown rock names count as no ground.

crystalline._note: Crystalline rock is very low, but its top fracturedMetres below the rock's top (under any cover) count as fractured: the weathered, jointed zone that hard-rock wells tap.

waterTable._note: Depth below the ground = minDepthMetres + k x (height above the drainage base) + desertDropMetres x dryness^2. The drainage base is the lowest water surface (sea 0 m, lakes, rivers) or ground within radiusMetres. k is the thickness-weighted class k of the top topMetres; dryness rises from 0 at humidAridity to 1 at desertAridity (precipitation / potential evaporation) and pulls k to 1. In humid climates a very-low or low layer starting within perchedWithinMetres under a more permeable one holds a perched table at its top, on ground at most perchedMaxHandMetres above the base.
waterTable._wetlandNote: Mapped wetlands (GLWD v2 as Core/WetlandGrid holds it, the grid the trees read: shares of 0.1 degree cells). The weighted share of the layers below is the cell's wetland; it lies on the cell's low ground (height above the drainage base, HAND: Renno et al. 2008 find waterlogged ground below about 5 m and uplands above 15 m; raised bogs stand higher). The table rises towards minDepthMetres by lift = min(1, share / wetlandFullShare) x (1 - HAND / wetlandMaxHandMetres), held to 0-1: depth - (depth - minDepthMetres) x lift, in any climate. Bog, marsh, saltmarsh, wooded peatland, swamp forest and mangrove are saturated ground; damp ground is saturated part of the year. Reads the grid only: no wetland, fire or tree rule changes.

salt._note: Salty: under the sea floor; under a salt flat (these cover recipes) or with a salt lake within the radius; deeper than brineBelowMetres below the ground; near the sea, deeper below sea level than ghybenHerzberg x the table's height above sea level (the fresh lens floating on sea water).

rating._note: samples x samples columns per chunk column. At each, the chunk's transmissivity T (m2/day) = the sum over its saturated ground blocks of the block's real thickness (m) x its class conductivity, halved at halfConductivityMetres below the ground; so the same ground reads the same at every vertical scale. The column's rating is log-linear in T between the transmissivity anchors [T, rating], which put Krasny's transmissivity classes (1993; Krasny and Sharp 2007: VI imperceptible below 0.1, V very low 0.1-1, IV low 1-10, III intermediate 10-100, II high 100-1000, I very high above 1000 m2/day) on the categories of HoD's prospecting pick (none up to 10, very poor 15, poor 20, light 40, moderate 60, heavy above). The chunk's rating is the mean over the samples x the recharge factor = rechargeFloor + (1 - rechargeFloor) x min(1, surplus / surplusFullMm); the surplus is precipitation minus evaporation from the Budyko curve (Fu, omega budykoOmega).
